THOUGHT: This 53-year-old male presents with a classic triad suggestive of Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS): (1) proximal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs) that paradoxically improves with repeated activity (“warm-up phenomenon”), (2) autonomic dysfunction (sluggish pupillary light reflex, dry mucous membranes), and (3) association with smoking-related malignancy — notably small cell lung cancer (SCLC), which is present in ~50–60% of LEMS cases. His 35-pack-year smoking history places him at high risk for SCLC. The weight loss (4.6 kg over 6 months) and chronic cough are red flags for underlying malignancy. Neurological exam findings — reduced deep tendon reflexes (Achilles 1+), initial 3/5 proximal leg strength improving to 5/5 after tapping (a hallmark “tap test” sign in LEMS), and sluggish pupillary reactivity — further support presynaptic neuromuscular junction dysfunction. Normal PFTs argue against primary respiratory muscle weakness or obstructive/restrictive lung disease as the cause of dyspnea or cough. The elevated voltage-gated calcium channel (VGCC) antibody — specifically P/Q-type — is highly specific (>90%) and sensitive (~85–90%) for LEMS. While myasthenia gravis (MG) also causes fatigable weakness, it typically involves ocular/bulbar muscles first, worsens with activity, shows normal or hyperactive reflexes, and is associated with AChR or MuSK antibodies — not VGCC. The improvement with exertion, hyporeflexia, and autonomic features strongly distinguish LEMS from MG. Other considerations (e.g., polymyositis, mitochondrial myopathy, or COPD) do not explain the warm-up phenomenon, autonomic signs, or VGCC antibody positivity.

DIAGNOSIS: Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome
